facts.title: A Green Twin Unmasked
facts.text: Praseodymium was discovered in 1885 by Austrian chemist Carl Auer von Welsbach, who split a substance called 'didymium' that had been mistaken for a single element since 1841. Didymium turned out to be two elements: praseodymium and neodymium. Welsbach separated them by tedious fractional crystallization, finally proving that the supposed element was an impostor.

facts.title: Named For Its Color
facts.text: The name comes from the Greek words 'prasios' (leek-green) and 'didymos' (twin), literally meaning 'green twin.' This refers to the distinctive green color of its salts, especially praseodymium oxide. Welsbach chose the name to honor both its hue and its origin as half of the old didymium pair.

facts.title: Tarnishes Before Your Eyes
facts.text: Fresh praseodymium metal is soft, silvery, and malleable, but it does not stay that way for long. Exposed to air, it forms a flaky, spalling green oxide layer that actually crumbles off and exposes fresh metal underneath to corrode further. Because of this, pure praseodymium is usually stored under mineral oil or sealed in glass.

facts.title: The Glassmaker's Goggles
facts.text: Praseodymium is a key ingredient in didymium glass, used in the safety goggles worn by glassblowers and welders. The element sharply absorbs the intense yellow light (around 589 nanometers, the sodium D-line) produced by hot glass and flames. This protects the wearer's eyes from glare and harmful infrared radiation while still letting them see their work clearly.

facts.title: Coloring Ceramics Bright Yellow
facts.text: When praseodymium is incorporated into a zirconium silicate crystal lattice, it produces a brilliant, stable yellow pigment known as praseodymium yellow. It is one of the most widely used ceramic stains for tiles and pottery glazes because it resists fading at high firing temperatures. The same element that makes green salts thus delivers a vivid yellow in ceramics.

facts.title: Magnets For Extreme Heat
facts.text: Alloyed with cobalt, iron, boron, and other rare earths, praseodymium helps make powerful permanent magnets. Praseodymium can substitute for part of the neodymium in neodymium-iron-boron magnets, improving their resistance to corrosion and to demagnetization at high temperatures. These magnets drive wind turbines, electric vehicle motors, and hard disk drives.

facts.title: Strength In Aircraft Engines
facts.text: Adding praseodymium to magnesium creates high-strength alloys prized in aerospace engineering. A famous example is mischmetal, a mix of rare-earth metals (largely cerium, lanthanum, neodymium, and praseodymium), which is alloyed into structural components and used in flints for lighters. Praseodymium's contribution improves strength without adding much weight.

facts.title: Light Through The Floor
facts.text: In specially prepared crystals, praseodymium has been used in experiments to slow a pulse of light to just a few hundred meters per second, and even to bring light effectively to a halt and store it. This is possible because praseodymium ions doped into a crystal have extremely sharp, long-lived energy levels. Such research points toward future quantum memories for storing and processing information with light.

facts.title: Forged In Dying Stars
facts.text: Praseodymium, like other rare-earth elements, is built up in the universe mostly through neutron capture inside aging stars and in the violent merger of neutron stars. Despite the name 'rare earth,' praseodymium is not especially rare in Earth's crust, occurring at around 9 parts per million, more abundant than elements like silver or gold. It is mined chiefly from the minerals monazite and bastnasite.

facts.title: One Stable Isotope, And Counting
facts.text: Natural praseodymium consists entirely of a single stable isotope, praseodymium-141, making it one of the relatively few elements that are mononuclidic. Every praseodymium atom you will ever encounter in nature has exactly 59 protons and 82 neutrons. Around 38 radioactive isotopes have been created in the laboratory, but none of them occur naturally on Earth.
